entryAnswer.explanation:
The snippet is a virtual file at examples/spending-alerts/__b121_entry_validation__.ts; it imports the private causal-occurrence sources with relative .js specifiers and creates no Graph, capability, binding or resource (per entry/task.json: given objects are supplied by the caller).

Validation before handoff. `handoffCausalCapabilities` calls `assertCausalCapabilities(graph, capabilities, expected)` before touching the recipient. That function is the exact issued-object gate: it looks the value up in the module-private `issued` WeakMap (capabilities.ts:51) and throws when there is no record, when `root.graph !== graph`, when `root.level !== "full"`, or when any of contract/implementationRevision/scope/epoch differ (capabilities.ts:72-82). A structural copy or a copied lower handle has no issuance record, so it is rejected; a capability issued by another Graph or under another binding/epoch is rejected too. It then re-checks lineage: each of identity/execution/retained must be issued to the same `instance` and `graph` (capabilities.ts:83-87), and the original identity relationships must hold — `full.execution.identity === full.identity` and `full.retained.execution === full.execution` (capabilities.ts:88-89). Because the throw happens first, the recipient callback is never invoked for an invalid capability; the README states the same rule: "A capability validation failure must be handled before passing the capabilities to a recipient; a structural copy is not an issued object" (README.md:41-43).

Identity-preserving delivery. The three levels are passed as the original frozen handles created by `createCausalCapabilities` (capabilities.ts:122-138), which freezes identity, execution, retained and full and registers each level in the WeakMap (capabilities.ts:140-146). The snippet reuses those references rather than rebuilding objects, so the `execution.identity === identity` and `retained.execution === execution` relationships survive the handoff. The framework example does the same: validate, then return `capabilities.execution` (causal-audience.examples.ts:18-25).

Does the execution level authorize arbitrary I/O? No. `ExecutionCapability` is only `identity`, `terminals`, `conservation` and `causalQuiescence` Node handles (capabilities.ts:27-32); it exposes no write, transport or publish method. The README says capabilities have no arbitrary I/O execution method (README.md:94-95), and the audience example comments that an execution view grants no I/O method (causal-audience.examples.ts:17). The only write in the package is the offline host's `lease.write(payload)` (causal-focused-host.ts:455), reached only after its guard verifies admitted effect, exactly one passing verification receipt, exactly one unrevoked local grant, matching epochs/digests and inbox readiness (causal-focused-host.ts:404-431), and even then success is only claimed when the returned byte count matches (causal-focused-host.ts:458-470). Possession of the execution level is therefore an observation/consumption right over identity, terminal, conservation and quiescence facts, not an authorization to perform I/O.
